system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-08-29 22:47:00 to 2179-09-01 13:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with primary sclerosing cholangitis and Child-Pugh class B cirrhosis was admitted after vomiting coffee-ground material, concerning for upper gastrointestinal bleeding. She had a history of esophageal varices and presented with a low-grade fever and mild hypoxemia. An EGD revealed high-risk stigmata on grade II varices, which were successfully banded. She remained hemodynamically stable throughout her stay, with no further bleeding. The fever resolved without a clear infectious source, and hypoxemia improved, attributed to atelectasis rather than hepatopulmonary syndrome, as confirmed by a normal bubble echocardiogram. She completed a course of prophylactic ceftriaxone for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and was started on sucralfate for mucosal healing. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue all home medications, complete a 14-day course of sucralfate, and follow up for a repeat endoscopy in four weeks.

procedures.long_title: Occlusion of Esophageal Vein with Extraluminal Device, Percutaneous Endoscopic Approach
Excision of Large Intestine, Via Natural or Artificial Opening Endoscopic, Diagnostic

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You came in after your endoscopy and colonoscopy today because you mentioned right upper quadrant pain. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m feeling okay. The pain was bothering me earlier, mostly on the right side under my ribs, but it’s better now. I wasn’t running a fever or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, that’s reassuring. We checked your labs, and your liver enzymes were a bit elevated—AST and ALT were higher than usual, and your bilirubin was up too. Given your history of PSC and past cholangitis, we wanted to keep you overnight to make sure this isn’t turning into an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I see. So you’re worried about another bout of cholangitis? But I don’t feel sick—no fever, no chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You don’t have the typical signs, which is good. That’s why we’re not starting antibiotics yet. We’re watching closely. If your labs improve and the pain stays gone, we can be confident it’s not active cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. What about the endoscopy? Did they see anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they saw some small to medium varices in your esophagus—some old banding scars and one medium-sized varix with red markings, which means it’s at higher risk for bleeding. They placed one new band on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So that’s why I’m on Carafate again? I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Carafate helps protect the lining and supports healing after banding. You’ll take it four times a day for two weeks. We also continued your omeprazole to reduce stomach acid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the colonoscopy? Everything okay there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The colon looked mostly normal, but they did notice slightly reduced blood flow in the lining. They took random biopsies to check for any early changes. Nothing urgent, but important for your long-term monitoring given your PSC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, because of the colon cancer risk. I’ll need another one in a few years, I guess?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your gastroenterologist will schedule your next surveillance colonoscopy based on those results. For now, we’re focused on your liver and the varices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I just reviewed your morning labs. Your bilirubin has already dropped from 2.6 to 1.6, and your AST and ALT are coming down too. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news! So the pain and the liver numbers were just a flare-up, not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks that way. Your blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria grew after 48 hours—which supports that. We think this was likely a temporary worsening of your PSC with cholestasis, not bacterial cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried I’d need IV antibiotics again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. You’re tolerating a regular diet, your vitals are stable, and your exam is benign—no tenderness in the abdomen. All signs point to discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my other meds? I’m on so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept everything consistent. You’re still on ursodiol and cholestyramine for your liver, spironolactone and furosemide for fluid balance, rifaximin and lactulose for encephalopathy prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my thyroid and mood meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, levothyroxine for your hypothyroidism, escitalopram daily, and temazepam as needed for sleep. All unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Any pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None at all. I’ve been walking a bit in the hall and feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your liver function is continuing to improve. We’re on track to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about the varices coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common in cirrhosis. That’s why we band them preventively. You’ll need a repeat EGD in six weeks to check healing and see if more bands are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the transplant list? Am I still active?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still listed. Your team is monitoring your status closely. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Final labs look good. Your bilirubin is down to 1.6, transaminases are trending down, and you’ve had no symptoms. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications as prescribed. Finish the full two weeks of Carafate. Stay on your low-sodium diet and fluid restriction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And watch for any warning signs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call your doctor if you develop fever, worsening abdominal pain, jaundice, vomiting, or black stools. Those could signal infection or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a repeat EGD scheduled in six weeks. Your transplant clinic will also be in touch. The biopsy results from the colonoscopy will be sent to your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are in. A prescription for Carafate has been sent to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing everything’s under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Keep up with your care plan, and we’ll keep monitoring you. You’re being discharged home in stable condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Continue meds, watch for symptoms, follow up in six weeks. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with primary sclerosing cholangitis and Child-Pugh class B cirrhosis was admitted for observation following a routine EGD and colonoscopy due to new right upper quadrant pain and elevated liver enzymes. She had no signs of infection, and blood cultures were negative. Liver function tests improved during the stay, and her pain resolved without antibiotic treatment. During EGD, one esophageal varix with red markings was banded prophylactically, and mild portal hypertensive gastropathy was noted. She remained hemodynamically stable, tolerated a regular diet, and was discharged home in stable condition with a two-week course of sucralfate and instructions to continue all home medications. A repeat EGD is scheduled in six weeks, and colonoscopy biopsies are pending.
